name: Evagrius Scholasticus
knownFor: Lawyer at Antioch and writer of a church history in six books, from the quarrel over Nestorius to the twelfth year of the emperor Maurice, written for the side that held to the Council of Chalcedon. He is a different man from the monk Evagrius Ponticus.
dates: Born about 536 by the reckoning of his English translator, E. Walford; Evagrius himself says only that he was a schoolboy when Chosroes took Antioch, and in his fifty-eighth year when he wrote of the plague. He ends his history in the twelfth year of Maurice, which Walford puts in 594. No source used here gives the year of his death
place: Epiphania on the Orontes by birth; Antioch, where he married and where Walford places his working life; Constantinople, as Gregory of Antioch's adviser

keyWorks.title: Ecclesiastical History
keyWorks.about: six books, from the rise of the quarrel over Nestorius to the twelfth year of Maurice; it tells the councils, the emperors, the Persian wars, the plague and the patriarch Gregory of Antioch, with passages on his own life

keyWorks.title: A volume of memorials, letters, decrees, orations and disputations
keyWorks.about: which he says he compiled, most of the memorials written in the name of Gregory of Antioch; Walford says it is lost

traces: His history carries the story of the church on from where Socrates of Constantinople and Theodoret end, Photius says, down to the twelfth year of Maurice.
Walford says Nicephorus Callistus used it in writing his own history.
Wilhelm Arndt and Bruno Krusch, editing Gregory of Tours, match stories in Gregory's books to stories in Evagrius.
remembered: Photius, patriarch of Constantinople in the 800s: "The style is not without charm, although somewhat diffuse; in matters of doctrine he is certainly more trustworthy than other historians."
Walford finds his style affected and his telling of wonders credulous, and says this should in no way harm his name for honesty.

uncertain: His years. Walford puts his birth about 536; Evagrius gives no year of his own birth, only that he was a schoolboy at the time of the Apamea display and in his fifty-eighth year when he wrote of the plague. Walford's page headings put the display in 540 and his wedding in 589; Evagrius dates the wedding by the year 637 of the era of Antioch. No source used here gives his death.

His side. He writes for the Council of Chalcedon and calls Nestorius "that God-assaulting tongue" and Eutyches "impious". He served Gregory of Antioch and wrote in his name, so his account of Gregory is a friend's.

His family. Evagrius says the plague took several of his children, his wife and many of his kin, and later a daughter and her son. Walford calls the wife his first wife, since Evagrius married again; Evagrius's own words say "my wife". No names are given.

The charge against Gregory. Evagrius says a banker accused Gregory of intercourse with his own sister, who was married to another man. Walford calls it a charge of incest. Evagrius gives no year for the hearing at Constantinople.
Gregory's years. Walford's headings put Gregory's election in 571 and his death in 594. Andrea Gallandi, in a notice reprinted by Migne, gives 570 to 593.
